FWIS 187.d: Students will engage critically with well-known and lesser-known artists to explore the 100+ year history of a uniquely American art form. After exploring the roots of the genre, students will explore its continued evolution to its present form to answer the question, “What IS country music?”
FWIS 187.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 219.d: We will read and discuss important historical and contemporary examples of “life writing”—memoirs, biographies, autobiographies, diaries, letters—and collect stories from friends, family members, or public figures. Our field experiences will be shared and workshopped, and we will use writing and/or visual storytelling to produce “unfinished memoirs” by the end of the semester.
FWIS 219.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 102.d: The blind spot of "the act of seeing" is its social construction, its ideological nature. This seminar unveils the various historical, political, economic, and social “filters” that condition our decoding of visual information. This writing seminar aims at developing skills to de-naturalize the "act of seeing."
FWIS 102.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 253.d: The course will focus on the life and thought of Socrates (469-399 BCE). The reading for the course will include several of Plato’s Socratic dialogues as well as Aristophanes’ Clouds, a wild comedy in which Socrates is mercilessly mocked for his outlandish uselessness and social destructiveness.
FWIS 253.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 138.d: This course approaches conspiracy theories comparatively and transnationally. We will examine how global events generate competing explanations that circulate across borders through digital media. From Lady Gaga and Beyoncé’s Illuminati connections to QAnon, transvestigation, and the Jewish International Order, this class will run the gamut of modern conspiracy.
FWIS 138.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 167.d: What is it about certain books that draws us in and keeps us turning the page? To answer this question, this class examines selected works of fiction and creative nonfiction with a focus on literary form, the psycho-social functions of narrative, and the physical and emotional experience of reading.
FWIS 167.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 159.d: This course examines and defamiliarizes ties of kinship—family, friendship, as well as chosen, symbolic and disrupted bonds—that shape human experience yet are often taken for granted. Through literature, film, philosophy, and theory, we will explore how these connections have defined identity and community across cultures and time periods.
FWIS 159.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 107.d: Using the film "The Matrix" as the point of reference, this course presents celebrated explorations of servitude and emancipation - from religious mysticism to Marxism and artistic modernism. Texts by Lao Tzu, Farid ud-Din Attar, Plato, Freud, Marx, Baudelaire, J.S. Mill, Proust, de Beauvior, Malcolm X, Marcuse, Baudrillard.
FWIS 107.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 276.d: Introduces performing arts of China, Japan, and Korea, like Noh, P'ansori, and Beijing opera, focusing on psychological and multimedia aspects. Introduces performance studies--how to think, write, and present ideas about singing, dancing, storytelling, and drama from perspectives like ritual, gender, music, choreography, costume, stage design, and literary criticism.
FWIS 276.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 141.d: Scientists communicate through articles, press releases, podcasts, and books. This course explores how scientific ideas transform across formats for different audiences. Students will examine how a discovery evolves into a research paper, news article, podcast, or graphic narrative, analyzing changes in the core message and its impact.
FWIS 141.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 181.d: This course examines the struggle for black representation in comics and graphic novels. We will discuss the unique opportunities that sequential narratives present to creators as they represent race on the page and we will examine the history of black artists working in the comic book industry.
FWIS 181.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 292.d: The 1920s were about new possibilities, aesthetic experimentation, and frenzied expression. We'll examine iconic '20s literature by Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Woolf, and others, as well as the linchpins of '20s culture: jazz, Prohibition, the Harlem Renaissance, and modern art. Highlights include lessons on the Charleston and a Roaring Twenties soiree.
FWIS 292.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 177.d: This course explores the forms and contexts of storytelling in Buddhism, with a broad eye toward literature, visual arts, and performance. Students engage in both creative and academic writing to understand the importance of narrative in Buddhist cultures and different approaches to writing in the modern day. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for FWIS 177 if student has credit for FSEM 109.
FWIS 177.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 202.d: The blind spot of "the act of seeing" is its social construction, its ideological nature. This seminar unveils the various historical, political, economic, and social “filters” that condition our decoding of visual information. This writing seminar aims at developing skills to de-naturalize the "act of seeing."
FWIS 202.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 278.d: Can reason show that there is a God? Does the existence of radical suffering give us good reasons to affirm atheism? Can religious commitment be rational? What is the relationship between God and morality? This class will focus on discussing and evaluating various sides of such questions--theism, atheism, etc.--fair-mindedly.
FWIS 278.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 289.d: In this course, we’ll explore how film and literature imagine the relationship between “femaleness” and artificial intelligence. From Siri and Alexa to Her’s Scarlett Johansson, we’ll consider why AI so often sounds female and what this reveals about gender expectations shaping—and shaped by—the artificial.
FWIS 289.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 166.d: Every year millions of college students leave their home countries to spend months, or even years, integrating into a new culture and interacting meaningfully with people in another country. This course explores significant features of international education, through reading, writing, and learning from experts.
FWIS 166.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 245.d: What is a museum? What role do they play in the modern world? This course fosters critical thinking about how and why museums were important institutions. They emerged as sites of identity within and between local, regional, national, imperial and global networks. Globally, a diverse number of museums are at once beloved and controversial, commanding and irrelevant. These contradictions aren’t new. To address the future of museums we must understand the evolution of these institutions in their global pasts. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for FWIS 245 if student has credit for HIST 244.
FWIS 245.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 134.d: This writing-intensive seminar examines Meiji period (1868-1912) women’s writings and what they tell us about women’s lives and cultural output at the start of Japan’s modern period. We will discuss fiction, speeches, diary entries, and newspaper articles and their historical, cultural, and literary contexts.
FWIS 134.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 281.d: This course examines the struggle for black representation in comics and graphic novels. We will discuss the unique opportunities that sequential narratives present to creators as they represent race on the page and we will examine the history of black artists working in the comic book industry.
FWIS 281.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 157.d: In this class, we will view some of the most influential films in the martial arts genre and read some of the classic sources that inspired their stories and philosophies. We will learn to think critically about audiovisual media and write stylistically aware, historically informed reviews and analyses.
FWIS 157.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 250.d: How did medieval Christians understand and treat mental and bodily illness? How did their experiences of pain, sex, childbirth, and death interact with larger concepts of God, nature, and the heavens? What role did angels and demons play? This seminar will explore these issues through close reading of medieval texts.
FWIS 250.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 113.d: This course offers an in-depth examination of the 2026 American midterm election with a focus on the election’s media and context. Students will critically engage with the developments of the final months of the election while analyzing the social and historical factors that shape the broader contours of American politics.
FWIS 113.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 153.d: This course explores how rhetoric and writing can impact romance and dating. Students will learn communication and critical thinking skills through reading and writing about romance, with particular attention to audience, context, and purpose. Our key course question is, How can writing and communication impact romantic and dating experiences?
FWIS 153.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 109.d: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of journalism through hands-on reporting and writing assignments produced in the working newsrooms of the Rice Thresher newspaper, Campanile yearbook, and KTRU radio. Students will produce stories for print, online, and audio formats, with social media integration.
FWIS 109.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 183.d: This course discusses utopias and dystopias across history and cultures through a political lens: national borders, imperial conquests, and modern urbanism all result from map-making and the power of human engineering to overcome or live in harmony with nature. Content includes films, essays, comics, novels, and more. All majors welcome.
FWIS 183.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 171.d: Science and technology, which have always transformed human society, seem to be doing so at an ever-increasing rate. By examining social theory, novels, and critique, this class asks: how do science and technology shape our understanding of ourselves, our culture, and our worlds?
FWIS 171.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 188.d: This FWIS will consider the personal essay as a vehicle for expressing and wrestling with one's humanity. We'll read the work of the first personal essayist, Michel Montaigne, along with contemporary essayists who've followed in his wake, examining how these writers reckon with their complex selves and our complex world.
FWIS 188.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 225.d: The course will examine the role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in students’ own composition education and prepare them to make informed decisions as consumers of this rapidly evolving technology. Topics include AI-assisted writing, AI ethics, and AI’s role in education generally and writing specifically. By the end of this course, in addition to improved writing skills, students will employ AI tools in their writing, evaluate some tools, and gain insights into how they are transforming education.
FWIS 225.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 270.d: The 1920s-30s witnessed an explosion of detective fiction, a genre still popular today. This course will read writers of the “Golden Age” (e.g. Agatha Christie) and ask questions such as: How does detective fiction work? Why did it flourish between the world wars? What does it show us about ourselves?
FWIS 270.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 130.d: In this class, we will explore E.M. Forster’s “The Machine Stops” and Jeanette Winterson’s Frankissstein, each of which lends itself to new questions about what it has meant to be human and how that meaning may be shifting.
FWIS 130.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 206.d: In this class, we will reflect on the stories that shaped us, read and analyze important children’s literature and the scholarship surrounding it, and submit proposals for our own subversive children’s books. We will explore the often ignored potential of children’s literature to unsettle the status quo and initiate change.
FWIS 206.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 272.d: This course examines key philosophical questions through the lens of superhero narratives—comic books, graphic novels, and films—that have become a powerful and enduring thread in popular culture
FWIS 272.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 110.d: In this course, we will look at graphic novels, memoirs, and comic books by writers and artists of the Asian diaspora. We will explore the ways in which Asian diasporic populations are historically marginalized and underrepresented, and how Asian diasporic graphic narratives work to counter misrepresentations, stereotypes, and prejudices.
FWIS 110.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 168.d: We will analyze buildings that ended up in legal battles. Problems include structural failures, design blunders and near disasters. You will write about what went wrong and why, who saved that day and who should have acted differently. You will learn to write critically and present a convincing argument.
FWIS 168.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 191.d: This course will approach American food writing, broadly defined, with a particular focus on anxieties, assertions, and perceptions of diversity in the American and global food systems: cultural diversity of foodways, impacts of dietary and agricultural practices on biodiversity, and differing technologies of food production, distribution, and consumption.
FWIS 191.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 106.d: In this class, we will reflect on the stories that shaped us, read and analyze important children’s literature and the scholarship surrounding it, and submit proposals for our own subversive children’s books. We will explore the often ignored potential of children’s literature to unsettle the status quo and initiate change.
FWIS 106.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 120.d: This writing-intensive course explores the possible link between reading literary fiction and empathizing with others. We'll read short stories, novel excerpts, and literary criticism in an effort to scrutinize and more deeply understand the specific elements of fiction that might provoke empathy.
FWIS 120.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 128.d: Covering movies ranging from the early 20th Century to the present day, this class asks students to think critically about what it means to depict the automobile through film and to consider how these depictions, and their meanings, might change in accordance with different historical, artistic, and political contexts.
FWIS 128.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 111.d: This is a course that uses the game of baseball as a prism through which to understand a complicated last 150 years of US history. It is a course about the place of baseball in American society and how the game both reflected and shaped/influenced American society. We will examine issues of economic growth and the rise of modern sport, race, gender, class, immigration, suburbanization, urban planning, capitalism, globalization and personal and community identity in American history using baseball as our analytical lens.
FWIS 111.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 163.d: This course explores the breadth and depth of Houston’s art world by examining a selection of art museums and galleries within and beyond the Museum District. For each site, we will consider its institutional history, mission statement, curatorial approach, and community engagement.
FWIS 163.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 179.d: What does the history of medicine look like when Asian experiences are emphasized? This writing-intensive seminar examines the history of health and disease in Asia and beyond. Topics covered include public health as both a political and practical concept; pluralistic medical systems; colonial and semi-colonial medicine; disease stigmatization; and pandemics.
FWIS 179.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 262.d: Love is an ancient philosophical problem. Writing about love means discussing politics, race, and sexuality, alongside psychology and biology. Our inherited ideas about love - how, who, and in what way, is it best to love? - are undergoing a revolution. Students will learn how to write to participate in these conversations.
FWIS 262.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 239.d: This course uses post-1979-revolution Iranian cinema to develop analytical, argumentative, and research writing skills. Iranian cinema is renowned worldwide for being artistic and deeply emotional, often thriving despite strict government regulations. The course is structured around seven film-based writing assignments, with class time divided between screening key scenes and discussion.
FWIS 239.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 280.d: Recently monogamy has been considered the norm. However, alternative relationship structures are gaining increasing visibility. “Relationship Structures” examines the diverse relationship styles of today. Writing about our individual connections with institutions and the state allows students to research the limits of interpersonal freedoms today.
FWIS 280.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 192.d: This course introduces students to the critical and historical study of science, technology, and medicine by investigating “The Scientific Revolution.” While the extent to which it is singular, scientific, and/or revolutionary continues to be debated, from 1450 to 1750, the world and how humans came to know, engage, and change it were dramatically and rapidly transformed.
FWIS 192.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 229.d: This course explores Heavy Metal music as a misunderstood yet globally popular genre, offering a compelling subject to study how music reflects societal concerns. Students will develop research and writing skills through readings and discussions in Heavy Metal and Popular Music Studies, practicing writing about music’s relationship with culture and society.
FWIS 229.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 103.d: This course will focus on historical art forms and their cultural context and aesthetic qualities. How does one put into words one’s ideas and feelings about something that is non-verbal? The course will cover a great range of art, including painting, photography, architecture, film, and even music.
FWIS 103.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 273.d: Star Trek reflects the rhetoric of the times and is itself also explicitly rhetorical. The franchise makes persuasive arguments about social issues and what values humans should pursue. This course will explore these rhetorical themes and allow students to focus on topics of their choice within the Star Trek universe.
FWIS 273.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 162.d: Love is an ancient philosophical problem. Writing about love means discussing politics, race, and sexuality, alongside psychology and biology. Our inherited ideas about love - how, who, and in what way, is it best to love? - are undergoing a revolution. Students will learn how to write to participate in these conversations.
FWIS 162.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 125.d: The course will examine the role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in students’ own composition education and prepare them to make informed decisions as consumers of this rapidly evolving technology. Topics include AI-assisted writing, AI ethics, and AI’s role in education generally and writing specifically. By the end of this course, in addition to improved writing skills, students will employ AI tools in their writing, evaluate some tools, and gain insights into how they are transforming education.
FWIS 125.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 184.d: Science is viewed as objective, but our perceptions of science are shaped by the language we use to describe it. This course explores the rhetoric of science communication, examining the challenges of simplifying complex ideas for broad audiences. Using audience-centered design, students will practice communicating scientific ideas across diverse genres.
FWIS 184.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 243.d: In this course, students will hone their skills of observation through careful study of nature, from the geology to the birds and plants of Texas. Students will learn how to interpret and communicate these observations through writing and illustration. This course will involve several local field trips to explore the natural history of the upper Texas coast.
FWIS 243.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 255.d: This course exposes students to the exercise of writing about Asian food. Students engage in the activity of "converting" multi-sensory experience, i.e. eating food, into writing on the one hand and think about transnational Asian food in the context of globalizing world. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for FWIS 255 if student has credit for ASIA 205.
FWIS 255.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 121.d: This course examines Hawai‘i’s role in shaping the U.S. Pacific empire. Students analyze how Native Hawaiians, Asian settlers, and diaspora communities navigated and resisted imperialism. Drawing on historical records, films, cultural artifacts, and secondary scholarship, students develop evidence-based writing skills to explore the intersections of empire, identity, and resistance.
FWIS 121.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 244.d: This course explores the biology of snake venoms, snakebite envenomation as a global health crisis, and venoms as a source of novel therapeutics. Students will develop skills to analyze scientific literature, develop a research proposal, and communicate their findings through written and oral formats.
FWIS 244.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 194.d: This course examines ways films have grappled with histories of dictatorship in Latin America, in the 20th century. We will use films alongside other historical and literary sources, to learn about various dictatorial regimes and explore broader questions about state violence, democracy, revolution, imperialism, justice, and memory.
FWIS 194.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 294.d: This course will explore the history of books and the material (both intellectual and physical) from which they are created. We will consider how the physical form of books has shaped their content and meaning and think critically about how contemporary media shape our reading, writing, and thought.
FWIS 294.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 178.d: Can reason show that there is a God? Does the existence of radical suffering give us good reasons to affirm atheism? Can religious commitment be rational? What is the relationship between God and morality? This class will focus on discussing and evaluating various sides of such questions--theism, atheism, etc.--fair-mindedly.
FWIS 178.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 201.d: This class focuses on the various ways that filmmakers have sought to represent the environment through film and television, while also considering the different "environments" that surround us. We will discuss diverse modes of filmmaking including documentary, genre cinema, and science fiction. Writing tasks will emphasize film analysis and criticism.
FWIS 201.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 275.d: What are ‘natural’ disasters? To approach this question, we examine the temporally, socially, and economically disparate layers of various disasters and consider the dynamic relationship between memory keeping and humanitarian aid. Our semester culminates in the production of a collaborative digital writing project that examines events in the Houston area.
FWIS 275.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 214.d: This course revolves around twelve objects that reflect the profound impact of the African diaspora in the Americas. From towering monuments to humble leather pouches, each artifact serves as a portal into the multifaceted tapestry of Black lives from the 16th to the 21st century, from the US to Brazil.
FWIS 214.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 249.d: This seminar invites students to read, reflect on, and write about the secret lives of fictional and nonfictional spies. Students will be introduced to a range of accounts about espionage, spanning the mid-twentieth century to the present. The assignments will allow students to practice writing for different disciplines and audiences.
FWIS 249.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 164.d: This course explores the act of walking, in theory and in practice. Through readings, discussions, writing assignments, and group and individual walks, it examines questions about the body and its movements; the construction and navigation of space; the tradition of travel writing; and the relationship between walking and thinking.
FWIS 164.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 204.d: This course will survey a variety of types of natural disasters that have–or could–impact much of the world. Special attention will be paid to recent natural disasters in the United States, but the course will also attend to disasters from far in the past and outside the US as well.
FWIS 204.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 241.d: This First-Year Writing-Intensive Seminar introduces students to applied sociological research through the study of social inequality, centered on education. Students analyze how evidence is produced, interpreted, and communicated, while developing skills in critical reading, data-informed argumentation, and clear, audience-focused writing.
FWIS 241.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 140.d: In the twentieth century and beyond, movies and television serve as an important source of mythologized national narratives (or somewhat “faked news”) from war movies, to westerns, to “biopics” of figures such as Kenneth Turing. Are their patterns of distortion at work, we can identify? How do we correct them?
FWIS 140.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 100.d: FWIS 100 introduces students to academic reading and writing through the study of a specific topic. In this course, students will acquire strategies to improve their critical reading comprehension and will learn how to enhance the clarity, style, and organization of their writing. Students will participate in group discussions and workshops, as well as individual consultations with Writing Coaches. Typical assignments include mapping an academic argument and summarizing a scholarly article. (This course does not fulfill the composition graduation requirement.)
FWIS 100.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 150.d: How did medieval Christians understand and treat mental and bodily illness? How did their experiences of pain, sex, childbirth, and death interact with larger concepts of God, nature, and the heavens? What role did angels and demons play? This seminar will explore these issues through close reading of medieval texts. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for FWIS 150 if student has credit for FSEM 171/MDEM 171/RELI 171.
FWIS 150.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 265.d: This writing-intensive seminar examines how and why the spread of disinformation has become increasingly more prevalent in our 21st century society and what impact it has on our democratic processes. We will take an interdisciplinary approach to discussing fake news, drawing from history, philosophy, journalism, media studies, and political science.
FWIS 265.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 137.d: Recent cultural movements encourage a more serious exploration of popular music. This course will participate by taking a critical look at what songs mean, what songs/albums/genres express, what our interest in music expresses, and how writing about music can lead us to great insights.
FWIS 137.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 186.d: What is “nature” and what does it look like in contemporary cultural representations? In this course, we will analyze texts and media objects—such as videos, film, posts and art works—that focus on nature as a subject.
FWIS 186.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 139.d: This course uses post-1979-revolution Iranian cinema to develop analytical, argumentative, and research writing skills. Iranian cinema is renowned worldwide for being artistic and deeply emotional, often thriving despite strict government regulations. The course is structured around seven film-based writing assignments, with class time divided between screening key scenes and discussion.
FWIS 139.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 288.d: This FWIS will consider the personal essay as a vehicle for expressing and wrestling with one's humanity. We'll read the work of the first personal essayist, Michel Montaigne, along with contemporary essayists who've followed in his wake, examining how these writers reckon with their complex selves and our complex world.
FWIS 288.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 248.d: This class is designed to introduce students to sports writing as a vehicle for conveying complex ideas and stories, and investigating difficult issues. It is not a sports journalism course, but rather one focused on story-telling through and about sports. We will read a variety of fictional and non-fictional writing about sports as a means to learning about how to look deeply into the world and the people around us.
FWIS 248.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 174.d: Sound surrounds us. And yet we often put little thought into what role it plays in our lives and the lives of our public spaces. This course aims to correct this oversight by offering an introduction to the field of sound studies focused on Houston’s audio environment, past and present.
FWIS 174.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 279.d: Scrooge, Sherlock, Elphaba, Dracula, Lizzie Bennet. Many of our favorite characters and our greatest stories exist in multiple incarnations across different media—books, films, cartoons, plays, games, theme parks, breakfast cereals. We will examine how stories change and use adaptation as a framework for studying story structure and genre.
FWIS 279.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 237.d: Recent cultural movements encourage a more serious exploration of popular music. This course will participate by taking a critical look at what songs mean, what songs/albums/genres express, what our interest in music expresses, and how writing about music can lead us to great insights.
FWIS 237.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 257.d: In this class, we will view some of the most influential films in the martial arts genre and read some of the classic sources that inspired their stories and philosophies. We will learn to think critically about audiovisual media and write stylistically aware, historically informed reviews and analyses.
FWIS 257.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 176.d: Introduces performing arts of China, Japan, and Korea, like Noh, P'ansori, and Beijing opera, focusing on psychological and multimedia aspects. Introduces performance studies--how to think, write, and present ideas about singing, dancing, storytelling, and drama from perspectives like ritual, gender, music, choreography, costume, stage design, and literary criticism.
FWIS 176.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 133.d: What makes life meaningful—and are we getting it wrong? In a culture of constant achievement and self-improvement, we sometimes wonder whether the lives we are building are actually worth living. In this course, we will explore purpose, fulfillment, and value through philosophy, literature, and film.
FWIS 133.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 145.d: What is a museum? What role do they play in the modern world? This course fosters critical thinking about how and why museums were important institutions. They emerged as sites of identity within and between local, regional, national, imperial and global networks. Globally, a diverse number of museums are at once beloved and controversial, commanding and irrelevant. These contradictions aren’t new. To address the future of museums we must understand the evolution of these institutions in their global pasts.
FWIS 145.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 172.d: This course invites students to consider whose stories we remember, and how/when/where. How does the framing of historical events bolster or disrupt dominant narratives of public memory? Students will examine scholarship on public memory and conduct analyses of the sites, sounds, and stories of national and local histories.
FWIS 172.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 119.d: We will read and discuss important historical and contemporary examples of “life writing”—memoirs, biographies, autobiographies, diaries, letters—and collect stories from friends, family members, or public figures. Our field experiences will be shared and workshopped, and we will use writing and/or visual storytelling to produce “unfinished memoirs” by the end of the semester.
FWIS 119.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 105.d: This course examines the nexus of media and politics in the present-day United States through a dual focus on political media (news and opinion coverage, political speeches, press releases, social media, and interviews) and the broader social and cultural context of American politics.
FWIS 105.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 267.d: What is it about certain books that draws us in and keeps us turning the page? To answer this question, this class examines selected works of fiction and creative nonfiction with a focus on literary form, the psycho-social functions of narrative, and the physical and emotional experience of reading.
FWIS 267.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 200.d: For transfer of an approved first-year writing intensive seminar. This course may not have been taken pass-fail at the transferring institution and must meet Rice University’s transfer credit requirements. Credit for this placeholder course will count towards the total credit hours required for graduation, and will be eligible to satisfy the university’s Writing and Communication Requirement. Transfer students must contact the FWIS transfer credit advisor to determine if their course will transfer. Instructor Permission Required.
FWIS 200.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 169.d: This seminar explores how the catastrophic events of the Holocaust, slavery, and apartheid continue to shape communities and individuals in Germany, South Africa, and the U.S. Students examine the challenges of reckoning with historical trauma and the healing power of the arts in a society at war with its past.
FWIS 169.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 269.d: This seminar explores how the catastrophic events of the Holocaust, slavery, and apartheid continue to shape communities and individuals in Germany, South Africa, and the U.S. Students examine the challenges of reckoning with historical trauma and the healing power of the arts in a society at war with its past.
FWIS 269.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 220.d: This writing-intensive course explores the possible link between reading literary fiction and empathizing with others. We'll read short stories, novel excerpts, and literary criticism in an effort to scrutinize and more deeply understand the specific elements of fiction that might provoke empathy.
FWIS 220.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 274.d: Sound surrounds us. And yet we often put little thought into what role it plays in our lives and the lives of our public spaces. This course aims to correct this oversight by offering an introduction to the field of sound studies focused on Houston’s audio environment, past and present.
FWIS 274.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 143.d: In this course, students will hone their skills of observation through careful study of nature, from the geology to the birds and plants of Texas. Students will learn how to interpret and communicate these observations through writing and illustration. This course will involve several local field trips to explore the natural history of the upper Texas coast.
FWIS 143.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 104.d: In this course, students will watch episodes of The Good Place paired with readings on the theories featured to explore “what we owe to each other” across a range of contexts, from every day communication to equity and access in writing and research in the students’ chosen field of study.
FWIS 104.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 215.d: This writing-intensive course introduces students to biological research and scientific communication. Student teams work on investigative projects with opportunities to ask questions, perform experiments, collect and analyze data, and share their findings. Recommended for students interested in the Biosciences major who have limited laboratory experience.
FWIS 215.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 260.d: In this course, we will draw on a range of disciplines, including anthropology, environmental studies, and indigenous studies, as we examine various indigenous environmental movements through the lens of foundational concepts such as land as pedagogy, indigeneity, and settler-colonialism. This course is aimed to (1) introduce specific case studies of indigenous leadership, knowledge, and innovation in environmental protection initiatives; (2) equip students with skills they need to critically analyze and compare various indigenous environmental movements; and (3) engage students in cultivating heathier ways of relating to land and indigenous communities.
FWIS 260.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 175.d: What are ‘natural’ disasters? To approach this question, we examine the temporally, socially, and economically disparate layers of various disasters and consider the dynamic relationship between memory keeping and humanitarian aid. Our semester culminates in the production of a collaborative digital writing project that examines events in the Houston area.
FWIS 175.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 290.d: In this class, we will be using Humes’ Garbology: Our Dirty Love Affair With Trash along with Alan Weisman’s The World Without Us, a projection of our planet without human-caused environmental degradation, to take stock of our own production of trash and depletion of natural resources and incite real change.
FWIS 290.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 108.d: This course will require students to read critically, discuss, synthesize, summarize and analyze writings about the contemporary affairs of the People’s Republic of China. The students will become familiar with a range of basic documentary sources in English – official press releases, government reports – and also popular and academic secondary sources.
FWIS 108.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 236.d: FWIS 109 examines film, television, novels and short stories in order to consider the American West from a variety of different perspectives and identities. In each case, we examine how alternate Western narratives intersect with, or refute, the dominant tropes and mythologies of this most contested of cultural spaces.
FWIS 236.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 293.d: Democratic societies claim to be based on the rule of law. This course examines what is required of a society that treats every individual equally regardless of a person´s status or influence. We will analyze the relationship of politics and the law in the distinct historical and national contexts of the contemporary US and post-war Germany, as well as exploring the topics of crimes, guilt, punishment and vigilante justice in selected literary texts and films.
FWIS 293.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 282.d: In the midst of a global climate and migration crisis, the safeguarding of borders has become an increasingly contentious issue worldwide. In this course we will explore the perilousness of the human condition, as experienced in the crossing of real and imaginary borders, and in the traumatic loss of homeland and self.
FWIS 282.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 123.d: This course will unpack the cultural legacy of the Star Wars films through traditional literary analysis and close reading, by situating the films historically, and by considering the ways that the films reflect attitudes towards a variety of social issues, such as spirituality/religion, philosophy, race, gender, class, nationality, and imperialism.
FWIS 123.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 242.d: Investigates ancient, historical, and modern cities and how their residents received water. Questions include: how cities developed water resources, how water shaped city life, and how the environment was engineered to produce water. Students will be able to choose a city and a water topic for their final seminar project.
FWIS 242.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 234.d: This writing-intensive seminar examines Meiji period (1868-1912) women’s writings and what they tell us about women’s lives and cultural output at the start of Japan’s modern period. We will discuss fiction, speeches, diary entries, and newspaper articles and their historical, cultural, and literary contexts.
FWIS 234.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 185.d: This class will delve into contemporary American poetry by exploring outstanding poetry books of the previous year. Students will study American poetry in literary and historical contexts, develop ability to analyze how poems "work," develop ability to create clear, effective prose, and build framework for exploring other types of poetry.
FWIS 185.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 101.d: This course will explore the mythology surrounding the Trojan war with regard to its original Homeric context, its cultural staying power, and the multi-medial representations of it that we continue to produce today.
FWIS 101.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 193.d: Democratic societies claim to be based on the rule of law. This course examines what is required of a society that treats every individual equally regardless of a person´s status or influence. We will analyze the relationship of politics and the law in the distinct historical and national contexts of the contemporary US and post-war Germany, as well as exploring the topics of crimes, guilt, punishment and vigilante justice in selected literary texts and films.
FWIS 193.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 195.d: This course introduces students to some historical and contemporary variants of nihilism via discussions of philosophy, literature, film, and art. It aims to help students see beyond these doomed views by providing them with an innovative set of perspectives and practices for successfully navigating an increasingly absurd world.
FWIS 195.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 240.d: In the twentieth century and beyond, movies and television serve as an important source of mythologized national narratives (or somewhat “faked news”) from war movies, to westerns, to “biopics” of figures such as Kenneth Turing. Are their patterns of distortion at work, we can identify? How do we correct them?
FWIS 240.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 261.d: This course covers over 200 years of Australian culture. We interrogate the many crises following the British invasion. Students will investigate settler colonialism, issues surrounding Indigeneity, democracy, and cultural change. We will read novels, newspapers, and archival objects to think critically about life in the colonies.
FWIS 261.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 263.d: This course explores the breadth and depth of Houston’s art world by examining a selection of art museums and galleries within and beyond the Museum District. For each site, we will consider its institutional history, mission statement, curatorial approach, and community engagement.
FWIS 263.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 277.d: This course explores the forms and contexts of storytelling in Buddhism, with a broad eye toward literature, visual arts, and performance. Students engage in both creative and academic writing to understand the importance of narrative in Buddhist cultures and different approaches to writing in the modern day.
FWIS 277.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 127.d: This writing-intensive seminar examines how medieval Arthurian literature has been re-imagined within 19th, 20th, and 21st century contexts. Beginning with foundational readings from Malory’s Le Morte d'Arthur, we will examine and discuss how the Arthurian tradition has been translated into various mediums, including the novel, comic books, art, and film.
FWIS 127.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 207.d: This course investigates US culture of the nineteen sixties by examining texts, such as Plath’s Ariel; films such as 2001: A Space Odyssey; and music such as The Beatles Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Heart’s Club Band.
FWIS 207.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 295.d: This course introduces students to some historical and contemporary variants of nihilism via discussions of philosophy, literature, film, and art. It aims to help students see beyond these doomed views by providing them with an innovative set of perspectives and practices for successfully navigating an increasingly absurd world.
FWIS 295.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 170.d: The 1920s-30s witnessed an explosion of detective fiction, a genre still popular today. This course will read writers of the “Golden Age” (e.g. Agatha Christie) and ask questions such as: How does detective fiction work? Why did it flourish between the world wars? What does it show us about ourselves?
FWIS 170.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 136.d: FWIS 109 examines film, television, novels and short stories in order to consider the American West from a variety of different perspectives and identities. In each case, we examine how alternate Western narratives intersect with, or refute, the dominant tropes and mythologies of this most contested of cultural spaces.
FWIS 136.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 230.d: In this class, we will explore E.M. Forster’s “The Machine Stops” and Jeanette Winterson’s Frankissstein, each of which lends itself to new questions about what it has meant to be human and how that meaning may be shifting.
FWIS 230.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 283.d: This seminar uses medieval visual and textual sources to explore how love, sex, desire, and gender were expressed across the Middle Ages. Through close engagement with medieval culture, it will reveal a world of far greater complexity than the myth of a rigid "Dark Ages" suggests.
FWIS 283.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 258.d: This writing course will introduce students to the theoretical debates about climate change, with a focus on social scientific and humanistic readings. In exploring climate crisis and the environmental justice, students will focus on close reading and practice critical writing skills.
FWIS 258.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 218.d: This course examines the experiences of mothering parents who do not fit prevailing ideals of “good” motherhood – mothers who are absent, single, young, sick. Together, we will experiment with engaged reading and writing practices as we explore cultural texts and essays from the fields of sociology, history, philosophy, and others.
FWIS 218.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 135.d: This course will explore the history of books and the material (both intellectual and physical) from which they are created. We will consider how the physical form of books has shaped their content and meaning and think critically about how contemporary media shape our reading, writing, and thought.
FWIS 135.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 210.d: By examining how historical subjects mis/represented themselves, students will think critically about identity and its construction, considering how membership and exclusion shape(d) societal perception and social hierarchies. Focusing on the 19th and 20th century United States, this course assesses historical impacts on contemporary perceptions and representations of identity.
FWIS 210.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 146.d: What is Apartheid? During the course, we will learn what Apartheid was and how white South Africans constructed and justified a system of racial separation, oppression, and violence in South Africa during the 20th century. We will also learn about the ways non-white South Africans fought against it.
FWIS 146.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 155.d: This course exposes students to the exercise of writing about Asian food. Students engage in the activity of "converting" multi-sensory experience, i.e. eating food, into writing on the one hand and think about transnational Asian food in the context of globalizing world. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for FWIS 155 if student has credit for ASIA 205.
FWIS 155.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 259.d: This course will focus on the three ballets Stravinsky composed for the Ballets Russes, which introduced Western Europe to Russian dance, music and art and became a seminal moment in the development of modernism.
FWIS 259.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 156.d: This course examines care and inequality in a world interconnected by histories and legacies of slavery, colonialism, and imperialism. In this class, we will read, discuss, and engage with ongoing movements to counter the systemic devaluation of care in the US and elsewhere in the world.
FWIS 156.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 131.d: This course examines the rhetoric and implications of the “War on Drugs” in the U.S. and Latin America. Students analyze from different perspectives key texts that are related to policies enacted in the last fifty years to suppress illicit drug use and that have affected civil liberties and national security.
FWIS 131.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 165.d: This writing-intensive seminar examines how and why the spread of disinformation has become increasingly more prevalent in our 21st century society and what impact it has on our democratic processes. We will take an interdisciplinary approach to discussing fake news, drawing from history, philosophy, journalism, media studies, and political science.
FWIS 165.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 231.d: This course examines the rhetoric and implications of the “War on Drugs” in the U.S. and Latin America. Students analyze from different perspectives key texts that are related to policies enacted in the last fifty years to suppress illicit drug use and that have affected civil liberties and national security.
FWIS 231.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 189.d: This course explores Heavy Metal music as a misunderstood yet globally popular genre, offering a compelling subject to study how music reflects societal concerns. Students will develop research and writing skills through readings and discussions in Heavy Metal and Popular Music Studies, practicing writing about music’s relationship with culture and society.
FWIS 189.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 144.d: This course explores the biology of snake venoms, snakebite envenomation as a global health crisis, and venoms as a source of novel therapeutics. Students will develop skills to analyze scientific literature, develop a research proposal, and communicate their findings through written and oral formats.
FWIS 144.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 190.d: In this class, we will be using Humes’ Garbology: Our Dirty Love Affair With Trash along with Alan Weisman’s The World Without Us, a projection of our planet without human-caused environmental degradation, to take stock of our own production of trash and depletion of natural resources and incite real change.
FWIS 190.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 148.d: This class is designed to introduce students to sports writing as a vehicle for conveying complex ideas and stories, and investigating difficult issues. It is not a sports journalism course, but rather one focused on story-telling through and about sports. We will read a variety of fictional and non-fictional writing about sports as a means to learning about how to look deeply into the world and the people around us.
FWIS 148.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 196.d: What makes a cultural product "Jewish," and what makes it "modern"? This course examines major works of Jewish thought and art from the nineteenth century to the present—fiction, poetry, film, philosophy, and visual art—exploring questions of religion, identity, memory, and the tension between universalism and particularism in modern Jewish culture.
FWIS 196.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 197.d: This class focuses on scientific skepticism and critical thinking, and how they can be utilized to distinguish science from pseudoscience. Core topics include the fallibility of perception; mechanisms of self-deception; as well as metacognition, cognitive biases and logical fallacies. These topics will be illustrated through examples of good and bad science.
FWIS 197.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 142.d: Investigates ancient, historical, and modern cities and how their residents received water. Questions include: how cities developed water resources, how water shaped city life, and how the environment was engineered to produce water. Students will be able to choose a city and a water topic for their final seminar project.
FWIS 142.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 211.d: We will discuss many ongoing debates over the content and meaning of quantum theory. This will reveal how theories are formed, how science is done, how these impact our day-to-day culture, and the surprisingly significant role that humans play in objective science.
FWIS 211.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 182.d: In the midst of a global climate and migration crisis, the safeguarding of borders has become an increasingly contentious issue worldwide. In this course we will explore the perilousness of the human condition, as experienced in the crossing of real and imaginary borders, and in the traumatic loss of homeland and self.
FWIS 182.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 221.d: From an aesthetic perspective, time travel has existed as long as there have been stories. Narrative introduces alien temporalities, transporting listeners and readers into different temporal landscapes. This writing-intensive course investigates the historical, aesthetic, and scientific connections between the authorial and scientific co-creation of time travel.
FWIS 221.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 129.d: This course explores key cultural, social, and political shifts in Africa from the late 19th century to the present, focusing on colonialism, independence movements, and globalization. Through literature, film, and critical texts, students examine African resistance, identity formation, and the continent’s role in global historical and political processes.
FWIS 129.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 205.d: This course examines various configurations of (what we today call) “queerness” across cultures, both ancient and contemporary. Engaging with a wide variety of texts across genres and mediums—myths, folktale, short stories, poetry, music, cinema, TV shows—we will study how conceptions of gender and sexuality vary widely between different historical and sociocultural contexts.
FWIS 205.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 246.d: What is Apartheid? During the course, we will learn what Apartheid was and how white South Africans constructed and justified a system of racial separation, oppression, and violence in South Africa during the 20th century. We will also learn about the ways non-white South Africans fought against it.
FWIS 246.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 124.d: This course will examine selected testimony given by Holocaust survivors. Their testimony varies according to time and the circumstance in which it was given and also according to the genre (film, memoir, drama) in which it is presented.
FWIS 124.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 149.d: Close reading of Homer's Odyssey, with a focus on what the poem suggests about different ways of using words, their effects on speakers and audiences, and their capacity to heal or harm. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for FWIS 149 if student has credit for CLAS 303.
FWIS 149.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 227.d: Medieval cathedrals are marvelous feats of engineering and wondrous works of art. This course explores various Gothic cathedrals, introducing students to their architecture, their programs of sculpture and glasswork, and the technologies that enabled their construction, as well as their relationship to learning, artistic expression, and political power.
FWIS 227.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 209.d: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of journalism through hands-on reporting and writing assignments produced in the working newsrooms of the Rice Thresher newspaper, Campanile yearbook, and KTRU radio. Students will produce stories for print, online, and audio formats, with social media integration.
FWIS 209.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 256.d: This course explores gossip as a powerful cultural force across literature, film, television, and media. From romantic intrigue to viral scandals, we examine how gossip intersects with gender, power, and truth across different global contexts. Special attention is given to the role of social media in shaping contemporary rumor and reputation.
FWIS 256.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 151.d: Do cats rule the internet? Why do we love capybaras so much? How come people in Mexico are hoarding axolotls in their purses? This course explores the ubiquity and meaning of animals in contemporary culture. Students will examine how animals appear in film, literature, social media, food systems, and science.
FWIS 151.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 173.d: Throughout the centuries, revivals of classical art and architecture have often accompanied cultural transformations prompted by both progressive and conservative intellectual or political movements. In this course students will learn different ways to view and interpret neoclassical art and architecture in today’s modern era to determine the context and purpose for using classical imagery. Mutually Exclusive: Cannot register for FWIS 173 if student has credit for FSEM 159/HIST 159.
FWIS 173.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 213.d: In this course, we will examine and analyze the meanings of supernatural stories—both historical and contemporary—set in the American South, as well as southern ghost tourism. In doing so, we will discuss what these stories tell us about southern history, culture, and ongoing debates over southern memory.
FWIS 213.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 132.d: This course will look at the ways major Hollywood (or equivalent) films have dealt with chattel slavery in the United States. We will explore the general question of how feature films deal with controversial historical issues by analyzing more specifically how Hollywood has dealt with American slavery.
FWIS 132.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 224.d: A philosophical exploration of the ethics of consent. What is consent, and why does it matter? When is consent valid? Must consent always be 'informed'? After examining these foundational questions, the course turns to consent in specific domains: sexual relations, medical treatment, and government. No philosophy background required.
FWIS 224.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 285.d: This course discusses utopias and dystopias across history and cultures through a political lens: national borders, imperial conquests, and modern urbanism all result from map-making and the power of human engineering to overcome or live in harmony with nature. Content includes films, essays, comics, novels, and more. All majors welcome.
FWIS 285.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 126.d: This course examines key philosophical questions through the lens of Black Mirror, the Netflix anthology series that explores the dark intersections of technology and human nature. Pairing episodes with philosophical texts, students will critically engage with issues that shape their daily lives.
FWIS 126.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 291.d: How exactly does the length of a piece of writing connect to its expression as a work of art and our interpretation of it? In this course, we’ll consider “shortness” as a challenge authors undertake, investigating the ways they weave complex tales into brief, often pithy, masterpieces.
FWIS 291.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 268.d: We will analyze buildings that ended up in legal battles. Problems include structural failures, design blunders and near disasters. You will write about what went wrong and why, who saved that day and who should have acted differently. You will learn to write critically and present a convincing argument.
FWIS 268.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 299.d: Divination, speculation, manifesting, gambling, investing: people have developed a diverse set of approaches to attempt to know the future and guarantee their fortune. Drawing from religious studies, science and technology studies, and socio-cultural anthropology, this course explores diverse traditions of prediction and manipulation: from magical practices to digital oracles.
FWIS 299.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 297.d: This class focuses on scientific skepticism and critical thinking, and how they can be utilized to distinguish science from pseudoscience. Core topics include the fallibility of perception; mechanisms of self-deception; as well as metacognition, cognitive biases and logical fallacies. These topics will be illustrated through examples of good and bad science.
FWIS 297.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 161.d: This course covers over 200 years of Australian culture. We interrogate the many crises following the British invasion. Students will investigate settler colonialism, issues surrounding Indigeneity, democracy, and cultural change. We will read novels, newspapers, and archival objects to think critically about life in the colonies.
FWIS 161.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 116.d: The narratives of travelers in the US are a window into history. Drawing on authors like Crevecoeur, Tocqueville, Trollope, and Kerouac, the class will discuss and write about themes such as Indian life and territorial expansion, democracy, slavery, civil war, western settlement, and 20th-cent. social movements. This course is eligible for credit toward the major in History.
FWIS 116.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 117.d: This FWIS course seeks to introduce Rice freshmen to the hidden layers of the story of the Americanization of the world in the twentieth century. The topics to be explored include the role played by private philanthropy in shaping and transmitting American cultural forms, the impact of the Cold War on the diffusion of American culture in such diverse arenas as literature, visual and performing arts, movies, TV programming and science and technology.
FWIS 117.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 286.d: This course challenges the myth of homogeneity in the understanding of East Asian societies by examining the experience of a variety of minority groups in terms of ethnicity, gender, religion, class, occupation, as well as physical and mental conditions.
FWIS 286.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 287.d: Students will engage critically with well-known and lesser-known artists to explore the 100+ year history of a uniquely American art form. After exploring the roots of the genre, students will explore its continued evolution to its present form to answer the question, “What IS country music?”
FWIS 287.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.

FWIS 115.d: This writing-intensive course introduces students to biological research and scientific communication. Student teams work on investigative projects with opportunities to ask questions, perform experiments, collect and analyze data, and share their findings. Recommended for students interested in the Biosciences major who have limited laboratory experience.
FWIS 115.restr: Enrollment is limited to Undergraduate, Undergraduate Professional or Visiting Undergraduate level students.
